title: Randomized medical-debt relief improves selected credit access but does not automatically repair health, care use, or financial wellness
source_unit: Participants in two randomized medical-debt relief experiments

observations.period: 2018 to 2020; two randomized medical-debt relief experiments

denominator.unit: people receiving randomized-experiment debt relief; experiment populations differ by arm

credit_access_surface.value: modest improvement when counterfactual reporting was active; no credit-report impact when it was not

observations.method: Two randomized experiments with RIP Medical Debt using credit reports, collections account data, and a multimodal survey; one experiment straddled an industry-wide pullback in medical-debt reporting.
observations.uncertainty: Selected downstream collection portfolios and study arms; results do not generalize automatically to all medical bills, care foregone, or household burdens.
observations.subgroup: People whose downstream medical debt had been or was about to be sent to collections.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit improvement depends on counterfactual reporting exposure and does not imply health or care repair.

denominator.unit: randomized credit-reporting subexperiment; published average effects

no_effect_when_reporting_absent.unit: no impact detected on credit-report outcomes

observations.method: Randomized debt relief compared with control accounts under counterfactual credit reporting versus a setting without that reporting exposure.
observations.uncertainty: Effects are average study estimates; credit access is not equivalent to realized borrowing, housing, work, insurance, or household welfare.
observations.counterinterpretation: A small score or limit change may not translate into usable credit or repair the underlying medical-cost experience.

denominator.unit: randomized hospital-debt experiment; published treatment-control contrast

another_unpaid_bill_sent_to_collections.unit: percentage-point causal increase; 6.6% of 16.2% control mean

interpretation.value: lower repayment of existing medical bills

observations.method: Randomized relief at the point hospital debt would otherwise be sold to a collector; collections account data track later unpaid bills.
observations.uncertainty: The result concerns existing bill repayment in the study population and does not establish intentional nonpayment, broader household insolvency, or health harm.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expectations of future relief, confusion about which debts were relieved, or debt targeting can produce lower repayment without a general moral-hazard conclusion.

observations.period: Hospital debt experiment survey follow-up; 2018 to 2020

denominator.unit: randomized hospital-debt experiment multimodal survey; published average effects

observations.method: Randomized debt relief with multimodal survey and administrative outcome follow-up.
observations.uncertainty: Average nulls do not rule out heterogeneous effects; the study does not observe care-foregoing origin, unpaid care, food/housing trade-offs, trust, or political action.
observations.counterinterpretation: Debt relief may still matter for credit or payment obligations even when average health and wellness measures do not move.

boundary: Randomized debt relief estimates selected downstream institutional outcomes; it does not complete the same-person chain from health need or skipped care to household adaptation, remedy, recovery, trust, or political action.
